set.notes: The document is ~870 pages and embeds survey imagery whose streams decompress to gigabytes, so extraction must stay in streaming mode with the oversized-stream skip enabled. UPDATED 2026-11-18 (research batch 9): RESOLVED. The lodged application was re-fetched (its SHA-256 matches the September manifest) and its appendices read as text; the pages cited are archived as excerpts. TITLE (Appendix B): registered owner 'WAMBO CATTLE COMPANY PTY LIMITED A.C.N. 058 718 326', 'LOT 125 CROWN PLAN DY316' (the record had DY516, a transcription error, corrected at its source). WATER (Infrastructure Services Report): 'There is no reticulated (town) water network in the vicinity of the site', so supply is on site; 'There is no anticipated continuous water demand for equipment cooling'; construction peaks above 300 kL/day; one building in operation about 16.5 kL/day. BACK-UP POWER: the air quality assessment says 'Five (5) 2.2MW diesel generators will be installed in each data hall, totaling 20 generators with a combined generation capacity of 44 MW', for 'network rooms and lift safety services only', tested 50 hours a year in all; the fire safety strategy says 'Generator Enclosures (8 per building)' and lists 186,336 litres of diesel. THE APPLICATION CONTRADICTS ITSELF. IT capacity: the planning report gives approximately 2,160 MW; the traffic assessment 'an ultimate capacity of 1,440 MW, delivered in 4 x 360 MW stages', and the economic assessment 'Total data centre IT load capacity of ~1.44 GW.' Ongoing jobs: the traffic assessment 'approximately 430 FTE at the ultimate 1,440 MW build'; the economic assessment '~1,400+ ongoing jobs'. Cost: the economic assessment gives '$14.5B excluding GST ($16B including GST)'; the record's A$31.9bn came in with the ABC's report (SRC_ABC_WD), not from the application. The ABC's 1.44 GW of IT capacity and 2.16 GW of total peak, as the seed row summarised it, read like the appendices; the planning report calls 2,160 MW the IT load and 3,240 MVA the total. PROPOSED to the author: SITE_WESTERN_DOWNS capital_cost_aud A$31.9bn (press) -> A$14.5bn excluding GST (the application's own figure); it_capacity_mw either kept at 2,160 (the planning report, which the row cites) with the conflict noted, or cleared until the applicant says which figure stands. Neither change is made by this pack.

set.notes: OPENED 2026-11-15. Macquarie's own IC3 Super West page, read for this batch, says 'IC3 Super West is currently under construction with the entire end-state power secured', gives '47MW IT Load' and lists the facility as 'Coming Soon'. SITE_MACQ_IC3 is named 'IC3 Super West (Macquarie Park)' and recorded operational on SRC_CERTSTRAT, a grade-C directory. The register lists 'IC1, IC2, IC3 and IC3e' as Certified Strategic Enclaves; IC3 East is operational at 12 MW IT load and is added by this batch as SITE_MACQ_IC3E. Which building each register name denotes, and whether a facility under construction can hold Strategic certification, is for a human. NO VALUE IS CHANGED HERE: the page is quoted against the existing row so the contradiction is on the record, not resolved by an agent. DECIDED BY THE AUTHOR 2026-11-18 (research batch 7): The author cannot say which building the register's 'IC3' is. It stays open. What would settle it: Macquarie Data Centres naming the certified building, or the Hosting Certification Framework's certificate scope. No value changes. UPDATED 2026-11-18 (research batch 9): Macquarie's own reporting settles the status, not the certificate. February 2026: 'Macquarie Park Data Centre Campus: IC2, IC3 East and IC3 SuperWest (expected to be completed by September 2026)'. 26 August 2026: 'Construction of IC3 SuperWest core and shell is complete, with the mechanical and electrical fit out progressing on time and on budget', 'Once completed, IC3 SuperWest ... will add an additional 47MW', and the results assume 'IC3 SuperWest Phase 1 revenue commences in 2H FY27'. So IC3 SuperWest was not operating at the end of August 2026. Its first phase is smaller than the building: at the topping out (3 December 2025) the operator said 'Phase 1 of the build is a ~$350 million investment and will deliver the complete core and shell with 6MW IT load fitted out'. The company's own names for the campus are IC2, IC3 East and IC3 SuperWest. PROPOSED to the author: SITE_MACQ_IC3 status operational -> under_construction, cited to the August 2026 results. Which building the register's 'IC3' certifies remains for Macquarie or the certificate to say.

set.notes: ADVANCED 2026-10-22 (research batch 3). Traced to source: Data Centres Australia told the inquiry operators 'will pay $10.3 billion in energy infrastructure to 2030, and $1.1 billion of that is excess capacity'. The report behind the industry's figures (Mandala, commissioned for Data Centres Australia by AirTrunk, AWS, CDC and NEXTDC) gives $3.1bn invested 2020-2025 and $7.2bn forecast to 2030, built from 'data from select data centre operators'; the two make $10.3bn, and the only '$10.3 billion' the report states is the Australian Government's grid funding. Its $1.1bn excess is within the forecast, with $0.5bn before. The networks told the inquiry the principle holds - Ausgrid: 'the customer who caused network costs pays for them'; Transgrid invests only on 'full commitment' and had no data centre commitment on 22 May 2026 - but none put a total on it. Still to test: the quantum against Transgrid, Ausgrid and Endeavour capital plans and AER determinations (aer.gov.au did not answer). UPDATED 2026-11-18 (research batch 8, second pass): Transgrid's own page states the principle and the constraint, not a total: 'Households and businesses should not bear the cost or risk associated with this growth'; capacity in the Sydney basin is 'largely exhausted'; since late 2024 it has received 'data centre connection enquiries totaling more than 10 GW within a 12 km radius of Sydney West'; capacity is allocated only on a signed connection agreement, for loads of 30 MW or more. It puts no dollar figure on what data centres pay. The AER's register closed the connection again today (recorded). The quantum test against the networks' capital plans stays open. UPDATED 2026-11-18 (research batch 9): Transgrid's letter to all data centre applicants of 20 August 2026 settles who pays for new capacity, not how much: about 1.5 GW of signed agreements in Western Sydney fit the existing network; beyond that 'Transgrid is unable to offer capacity ... unless the appropriate network augmentation is undertaken with the connection'; augmentation 'could unlock up to 2 GW'; and 'the costs of those augmentations will be borne by the data centre proponent creating that need rather than electricity consumers more broadly'. Enquiries exceed 20 GW. No dollar figure is given, so the $10.3bn claim is still untested against the networks' own numbers.

set.notes: ADVANCED 2026-10-22 (research batch 3). The free routes give the sector's and the government's word, not a revenue office's: Data Centres Australia told the inquiry 'Data centre operators do not receive subsidies or tax incentives' (1 May 2026); the BCA's Submission No 116 says operators 'pay full taxes with no concessions'; the Secretary of the Premier's Department said 'The one thing that we don't contemplate is government participation financially' (22 May 2026). What the State does give is in kind: the IDA ($17.7m in the 2025-26 Budget) and the Guidelines' concierge. No witness from Revenue NSW appeared. GIPA-002 to the Department of Customer Service (which holds Revenue NSW's records) is drafted from reports/RG007_foi_strategy.md; the Victorian, Queensland and Commonwealth templates stay in that file. UPDATED 2026-11-18 (research batch 8, second pass): The free substitute is refused: the 2026-27 Budget Paper No. 1, which carries the tax expenditure statement (Appendix C), sits under a path nsw.gov.au's robots.txt disallows; the older budget.nsw.gov.au links now redirect. Recorded; BLOCKED on download #30 (and GIPA-002, not lodged). UPDATED 2026-11-18 (research batch 8, the author's downloads): NSW PART, from the State's own statement (download #30). Budget Paper No. 1 for 2026-27 estimates '$16.8 billion' of tax expenditures and concessions and itemises every one over $1 million: its Appendix C never mentions data centres. Data centres appear elsewhere only as a driver of business investment and in Sydney Water's strategy for 'servicing data centres', which 'is supported by principles of full cost recovery'. So no data-centre concession of $1 million or more is in the NSW statement; a firm-level grant below that line, or one made outside the tax system, is not excluded (GIPA-002, not lodged). Other states remain. UPDATED 2026-11-18 (research batch 9): QUEENSLAND: the 2026-27 Budget Strategy and Outlook carries the State's tax expenditure statement and never mentions data centres (checked by this pack's script). VICTORIA: Budget Paper No. 5 is hosted where the crawler's robots check fails (recorded); download #35. Still unread: WA, SA, Tasmania, the ACT and the NT.

set.notes: ADVANCED 2026-10-30 (research batch 5). SURVEY: the attachment index of 6,866 documents across the NSW data centre records holds three donation disclosures. ROBERTS ROAD (SSD-10330): image-only, read by OCR and by eye - the company's director and chief executive, as applicant, declared $7,500 to the Liberal Party of Australia - NSW Division on 18 June 2018 (signed 2 December 2019, filed with the EIS). The Department's assessment report says the delegation applied where 'a political disclosure statement has not been made' and that no reportable political donations were made by the Applicant in the last two years; a delegate decided it. Why the disclosure did not change who decided is not on the record. TALAVERA ROAD (SSD-24299707): Macquarie Telecom gave $2,000 and $1,500 to the Liberal Party NSW Division and $1,980 to a City of Ryde West Ward campaign group in 2020-21; with Ryde's objection, that made the Commission the consent authority. MAMRE ROAD (SSD-92743706): restricted. Next: the NSW Electoral Commission's disclosure register (not yet tried) and GIPA-003. No improper conduct is alleged or implied. BLOCKED on download #34 (and GIPA-003, not lodged). CDC, AirTrunk, NEXTDC, Equinix, Goodman and Stockland are not on it. ADVANCED 2026-10-14. Archived and read the article itself (version of 2026-10-02; it was not archived when first read on 2026-09-18, so that version cannot be shown): it does not mention Vantage, AustralianSuper, AirTrunk SYD3 or Stockland, so the two entities' claims are withdrawn and the two sites now take their better sources as primary. Re-sourced to the register: the provider counts in the Equinix, Digital Realty, Macquarie (now six sites, adding IC3e), DCI and Telstra notes, the framework's 'highest level of assurance' wording, and the Macquarie security record, which is derived from the register and now VERIFIED. The four capacity metrics it relays from Mandala and CBRE drop to low confidence. Marsden Park's application row now cites the portal and its assessment report. The Mandala report the article names (Data Centres as Enabling Infrastructure, November 2025, archived) does not state 1,350 MW or 3,100 MW, in megawatts or gigawatts, in its text (pages 46 and 47 of its 48 carry no text and were not read as images); it points to Mandala's October 2024 report, which this environment cannot fetch because the host's robots.txt refuses it, as does CDC's copy. CBRE answers 403. FROM THE ARCHIVED REGISTER (primary, SRC_HCF_REGISTER): its text names only 'the Department' and the page carries the Department of Home Affairs logo (corrected 2026-10-21: earlier notes overlooked the logo); it lists data centre facilities that match no site record here: Cloud Carrier DB1 (facility); Vocus TransACT House Dickson (enclave). RG-096 matched only existing records, so these are candidates for new site rows. LEADS ONLY, from search-engine summaries read on 2026-10-14 (below grade D, not relied on, and kept out of every fact row): the framework appears to have moved from the Digital Transformation Agency to Home Affairs on 1 May 2023 (the move and its date, not the current branding, are the lead); the 1,350 MW and 3,100 MW figures appear to come from Mandala's October 2024 report; and AustralianSuper appears to have announced a EUR 1.5bn minority investment in Vantage Data Centers' EMEA platform on 11 September 2023. UPDATED 2026-11-18 (research batch 8, second pass): The two Mandala figures now rest on Mandala: the October 2024 report says 'data centre deployable capacity in Australia is projected to more than double from 1,350 megawatts (MW) in 2024 to 3,100 MW by 2030', and that it 'was commissioned by AirTrunk, Amazon Web Services, CDC, Microsoft, and NEXTDC'. Read from the copy AirTrunk publishes; Mandala's own host had refused. The two metrics are re-sourced to it (REPORTED, medium: an industry-commissioned projection). STILL ON CertifiedStrategic.com alone: the two CBRE figures (CBRE answered 403) and the national count of certified facilities. UPDATED 2026-11-18 (research batch 9): What rests on CertifiedStrategic.com alone is now the two CBRE figures (live capacity 1,400 MW in 2025 and 1,800 MW by 2028), with CBRE's site refusing the crawler. The national count of certified facilities also still cites it, but that metric is already at low confidence and marked superseded by the count taken from the register itself (hcf_certified_strategic_register); the Mandala figures are re-sourced. PROPOSED to the author: keep the two CBRE metrics at low confidence as reported second-hand, or retire them.
